I have been farming this land for fifty years — I count from the day I first toddled after my father into these fields, and I have never known another life. With only 4.1 mu, I cannot afford mistakes. Wheat-maize double cropping is my backbone: it feeds my household of three and brings steady cash, so I will put 3.5 mu into that rotation. After the autumn harvest of maize, I will rotary till and sow improved wheat seed. I will apply about 50 kg of nitrogen per mu, along with phosphate and potash, because the seed-shop man and my neighbors all say this is what the high-yielding varieties need. I will irrigate three times from my well — before winter, at jointing, and at grain filling — and spray four times for weeds and insects. In early June, as soon as the wheat is threshed, I will plant hybrid maize on the same 3.5 mu without ploughing; there is no time to waste in the summer heat, and no-tillage has always worked for me. I will give the maize about 20 kg nitrogen per mu, irrigate twice when the rains fail, and spray three times. The remaining 0.6 mu near the house I will keep in cotton. Cotton prices have been decent, but it is back-breaking work — fourteen pesticide sprays and two irrigations — which is why I only keep a small patch. I will rotary till that plot, plant improved cotton seed, and expect around 550 kg of seed cotton per mu. My wife works off-farm, so labor is tight, but I know these crops and this well, and I will manage them the way my father taught me.
